strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 8 public 2D/3D embodied reasoning benchmarks, 4 newly introduced primitive benchmarks (Where2Go/Fit/Approach/Grasp), object navigation on HM3D/MP3D, simulator-based end-to-end evaluation across 3 progressive task tiers, and qualitative real-robot deployment examples.

OmniEVA achieves strong quantitative results, outperforming substantially larger general-purpose models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro) and specialized 3D-LLMs on most benchmarks despite an 8B parameter backbone.

Reasonable ablation studies isolating the contribution of the gated 3D router (vs. hard-coded and no-3D baselines) and of the TE-GRPO training strategy (task-only vs. task+embodiment reward), with both quantitative results and interpretable qualitative case studies (gate activation words, placement examples).

The two-stage training pipeline (SFT warm-start + curriculum-scheduled GRPO with task/embodiment rewards) is a sensible and clearly motivated design for bridging semantic correctness and physical executability.

Large, well-documented training data curation (~5.2M samples across general, image, video, 3D reasoning) with detailed appendix descriptions, which aids reproducibility of the data pipeline even if the model/weights are not released.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core technical components (Gumbel-softmax gating/MoE-style routing between 2D and 3D tokens, GRPO with shaped rewards) are established techniques recombined for this application; the embodiment reward (EvalExec) is only vaguely described ("validating the plan against robotic constraints such as kinematics, reachability") without a precise formal definition or simulator details, hurting reproducibility.

Potential evaluation circularity: the in-house primitive benchmarks (Where2Go/Fit/Approach/Grasp) are constructed by the same team that curates the "Custom Embodied Task Dataset" used for SFT warm-start and RL training, and the paper does not clearly establish disjointness between training distribution/construction pipeline and the evaluation sets, raising concerns about inflated performance from distributional match rather than generalization. These test sets are also small (200-464 samples).

Table 1 ablation shows the proposed dynamic 3D integration slightly underperforms hard-coded 3D integration on ScanQA (30.78 vs 31.46), and the overall average gain (1.22%) is modest, weakening the generality claim of the gated router.

Some baseline scores on the introduced Where2Approach benchmark are implausibly close to zero for multiple strong general models (e.g., 0.17-3.5), which is suspicious and could indicate output-format mismatches rather than a genuine capability gap, undermining the fairness of this comparison.

Real-world deployment evidence is thin and purely qualitative (two prompt examples across two figures), with no quantitative success rates, trial counts, or failure analysis, despite the paper's central claims about real-robot executability.

Missing methodological details: how ground-truth gate labels (o^label) for TAGR pretraining were obtained is not explained; the curriculum coefficient λ_t schedule is described only qualitatively; no variance/multiple-seed reporting is given for any experiment.

The paper makes several strong "first-to" novelty claims (first dynamic 3D-grounding router, first embodiment-aware GRPO) without deep engagement with closely related MoE-style multimodal fusion or constrained RL-for-robotics literature, which could overstate the contribution.

Noticeable lack of polish: stray leftover text in the appendix ("huozh"), typos ("Moile Placement", "fist determine"), and inconsistent notation, suggesting the manuscript would benefit from another proofreading pass.

strengths: Broad and comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 2D and 3D embodied reasoning benchmarks (Where2Place, VSI-Bench, PACO-LVIS, RoboRefit, SQA3D, ScanQA, Scan2Cap, ScanRefer) as well as navigation (HM3D/MP3D), showing consistently strong or SOTA numbers against sizable general and embodied-specialist baselines.

The idea of task-adaptive, gated selective fusion of 3D positional information (rather than static/hard-coded 3D injection used in prior 3D-LLMs) is a sensible and interpretable design, supported by qualitative analysis of gate activation patterns (Figures 4-5) that align with intuitive linguistic cues.

The two-stage training pipeline (SFT warm-start + TE-GRPO with task and embodiment rewards and a curriculum schedule shifting from semantic to embodiment-feasibility reward) is a reasonable attempt to bridge semantic correctness and physical executability, and the ablations in Figure 6 show clear benefits of the proposed reward components on primitive and downstream tasks.

Extensive appendix with dataset composition (5.2M samples), detailed benchmark construction protocols, hyperparameters, and many qualitative examples, which aids reproducibility and transparency of the data pipeline.
Includes end-to-end simulated and limited real-robot deployment demonstrations, going beyond pure offline VQA-style evaluation that dominates much prior work in this space.
weaknesses: The central ablation justifying the Task-Adaptive Gated Router (Table 1) shows only a marginal average improvement (+1.22% over hard-coded 3D fusion) and the dynamic method actually underperforms the hard-coded baseline on ScanQA (30.78 vs 31.46), undermining the core claim that selective/gated 3D fusion is clearly superior to naive fusion.

Several of the primitive 'embodied' benchmarks used for the central comparisons (Where2Go, Where2Fit, Where2Approach, Where2Grasp) are self-constructed by the authors and also appear to be closely related to the custom training data distribution used to train OmniEVA, while baselines (GPT-4o, Gemini, RoboBrain, etc.) are evaluated zero-shot; this creates a substantial in-domain advantage for the proposed model and makes the large reported margins (Table 2, Figure 6) difficult to interpret as genuine capability gains rather than benchmark/training-distribution alignment.

Real-world robot validation is extremely thin: only two qualitative example trajectories (Figures 10-11) are shown, with no quantitative success rates, no trial counts, no baseline comparisons, and no failure analysis, despite the paper's repeated emphasis on 'real-world robotic execution' and 'significantly improving success rates on real robots' as a key contribution.

The embodiment reward EvalExec(q, o) is only vaguely described ('validating the plan against robotic constraints such as kinematics, reachability, and environment limitations within simulator') without specifying which simulator, how the reward is computed at scale during RL, or its fidelity/cost, leaving a core technical component underspecified and hard to reproduce.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the gated router is essentially a lightweight MoE-style binary gate over a frozen pretrained backbone (InternVL3-8B) combined with a sentence-transformer encoder, and TE-GRPO is a fairly direct extension of GRPO with additional reward terms and a curriculum weighting schedule; the conceptual building blocks (Gumbel-softmax gating, GRPO, curriculum reward shaping) are all well established in the literature.

Some reported percentage improvements (e.g., 'Where2Approach and Where2Fit exhibit performance gains of 28.95% and 34.28%') are not clearly specified as absolute or relative, creating ambiguity about the actual magnitude of improvement claimed from TE-GRPO.

Qualitative failure cases in the appendix (e.g., 3D visual grounding failures, scene imagination errors, inconsistent predictions on ScanQA-style questions) are presented without systematic quantitative failure-mode analysis, limiting insight into the method's actual robustness and limitations.

No variance/error bars, multiple-seed results, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere, making it difficult to assess whether the often small performance differences over baselines are meaningful.

strengths: Addresses two clearly motivated and under-explored limitations in MLLM-based embodied reasoning: the 'geometric adaptability gap' (static/hard-coded 3D fusion) and the 'embodiment constraint gap' (plans that are semantically valid but physically infeasible).

The Task-Adaptive Gated Router (TAGR) is a well-motivated, interpretable mechanism: it is conditioned on both task semantics and scene complexity, uses Gumbel-Softmax for differentiable gating, and is accompanied by a convincing qualitative/quantitative analysis (Fig. 4-5) showing it activates on geometry-related vocabulary and deactivates on counting/color queries.

TE-GRPO is a reasonable extension of GRPO that explicitly incorporates task-completion and embodiment-feasibility rewards with a curriculum schedule (lambda_t), and the ablation in Fig. 6 shows sizable gains on Where2Approach/Where2Fit and downstream Mobile Placement/Pickup tasks when both reward terms are used together.

Broad empirical coverage: 8 public 2D/3D embodied-reasoning benchmarks, 4 new primitive benchmarks (Where2Go/Fit/Approach/Grasp), 3 simulator-based end-to-end evaluation suites (object seeking, mobile manipulation, delivery), and qualitative real-robot deployment, giving a fairly holistic picture of the system.

Strong quantitative results: SOTA on 7/8 standard benchmarks despite a comparatively small 8B backbone, including a notable text-only (no detector/grounding head) 3D visual grounding result on ScanRefer that surpasses a dedicated 3D grounding method.

Extensive, well-documented appendix covering architecture/training hyperparameters, dataset composition (~5.2M samples), benchmark construction protocols, and many qualitative examples, which aids reproducibility and understanding of the pipeline.
weaknesses: The core TAGR contribution shows only a modest average improvement (+1.22%) over hard-coded 3D fusion in Table 1, and actually underperforms the hard-coded baseline on ScanQA (30.78 vs 31.46), which somewhat tempers the claimed superiority of dynamic gating over static fusion.

The four new primitive benchmarks (Where2Go, Where2Fit, Where2Approach, Where2Grasp) and the simulator-based end-to-end benchmarks are authored in-house with fairly small sample sizes (e.g., 207, 464, 200, 200 examples) and are evaluated with little-to-no comparison against strong external baselines beyond the paper's own ablations/RoboBrain, raising concerns about benchmark validity, potential evaluation bias, and statistical robustness of reported gains.

Real-world robot validation (Appendix F) is purely qualitative (two illustrative trajectories with photos); no quantitative success rate, failure analysis, or comparison to baselines is reported for physical deployment, which weakens the central claim that TE-GRPO training meaningfully improves real-world executability.

The embodiment-feasibility reward (EvalExec) is computed via simulator-based constraint checking during RL; the extent of sim-to-real gap and how well simulated embodiment rewards transfer to the real dual-arm platform is not analyzed quantitatively.

Baseline comparisons in several tables mix models of very different scale and training regimes (e.g., 7B/8B vs 32B, general MLLMs vs specialized 3D-LLMs), making some comparisons less apples-to-apples, and the paper does not report variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics for its main results.

The paper's own analysis shows that when the downstream low-level control policy is a bottleneck (e.g., Mobile Pickup), the gains from r^embod are muted, suggesting the embodiment-aware reasoning improvements may not straightforwardly translate into end-task success in more complex real settings.

Minor clarity/presentation issues (e.g., 'Moile Placement' typo, stray text fragment 'huozh' in Appendix A, some dense notation) and no explicit statement in the main text regarding release of code/benchmarks for reproducibility, despite a referenced project page.
